title: Fingerprints are the new cookies (royfish.dev)
comments: Every time this resurfaces I like to remind people that this is mostly impractical and not how things actually work at the commercial level.Just because someone can theoretically demonstrate your fingerprint today doesn't mean you have the same fingerprint in a few days. It's that kind of stability that you actually need for consistent matching for advertising or tracking purposes.90% of commercial fingerprinting services still rely mostly on the IP address. Once you remove the IP address, you're left with a set of configurations that have a very short half life - volume settings, installed fonts, software versions, etc. You can expect a good portion of your audience to degrade within a couple of days. (Whereas a cookie has a life of 2 years - practically though they only survive a few months).What you actually pay for from third party vendors is a connection made around a more stable data point - a phone number, an email address, a user ID, etc. With one of these data points you can actually track people across multiple devices for as long as you want.reply
IMO,  data brokering is what should be illegal, not the cookie .reply
The problem with this is the biggest, most important, and sketchiest data brokering services (credit monitoring) are all but entrenched in law at this point.reply

Overall correct, but you're kind of missing some of the cat-and-mouse details for fingerprinting centered around infosec and anti-fraud purposes rather than generic ad-related tracking. That stuff can get way more intense, and is constantly changing based on new techniques developed, countermeasures from cybercriminals, and mitigations from browser developers.reply
on what basis do you believe this about fonts? my guess would be that the average user doesn’t install or remove fonts often if ever, but it’s only a guessreply

I don't actually know how much this happens - software versioning is the biggest one. Chrome updates every two weeks, Microsoft updates once a month, your GPU drivers get updated semi regularly, etc. Any one of those would break the fingerprint.reply
Most people probably have completely default fonts, right? Doesn't seem like much of an identifier anywayreply
Hmm. I used to have to do that a lot, but I haven't in a few years now.reply

I've seen anti-fingerprinting plugins and browser configs, etc, but they all seem to make you more interesting for not being fingerprintable, or for turning off a lot of features used in fingerprinting.Is there any reason a browser or plugin couldn't just spoof the data used in fingerprinting to random values? So it emits different values for each page or resource you load?reply

Random is often going to be indirectly fingerprintable too, since some values are always the same (or the same given each browser version). Some values can't be set to be random or otherwise non-fingerprintable data without affecting the user, like viewport size.Spoofing 'Newly installed most recent version of Google Chrome on the latest version of Windows 11 in the US' without leaving any holes revealing something fishy is surprisingly hard, but that or 'Safari running on recent-ish iPhone running up to date iOS' would be the ideal target to blend in with the crowd.reply

title: Doory – Open-Source Canva (github.com/shaongitbd)
comments: So with this future of vibe coded tools , how to choose which one to use?reply

A lot of what makes Canva stand out comes from its IP coupled to their ecosystem/product (templates, assets and stock photography), its otherwise a pretty simple tool with basic functionality (but with good UX) compared with more professional software like photoshop or illustrator, or Figma. I'm sure you can built an open source equivalent in terms of software, but I don't think it's really possible for open source to produce a true replacement or alternative.THAT ASIDE, it might be worth focusing on UX. This looks vibe coded, maybe it isn't.- The UI is broken in a few places (the tools text in the shapes menu)- Consider prioritising more important tools based on available space in the ui, the header is a bit cluttered.- Some of the tool menus are awkward to use, like in Canva those are in a side bar and when they open the have panels that don't disappear when their parent looses focus. Probably worth making sure you're not using their exact icons as well as these look pretty similar.- Your add page button is creating an awkward scroll which you could probably limit by exposing add page in a way that didn't do that. Maybe remove the add page button below the canvas,  as you already have an add page button in the bottom left, you should have more vertical space for the design as a result.- You've got several different export sharing options in the header side by side. Might be worth collapsing that into a menu to minimise clutter. Both tools like canva and more professional tools layout their UIs like this. By all means do don't it just because they are, but there is some rational here why they would.- There are two places in the header that talk about the save state on the left and the right (one saying saved, the other saying saved in the browser). Consider having consolidating that.- do you really want to place the copy "Sign up to keep it forever" next to the sign up button? do you have any reason this is likely to stand out from the rest of the UI features there? I reckon if not get rid of it. Or if it's that important get rid of anything competiting for its attention which right now is a lot of things.- you have a ellipses for a menu with a ton of options, in most software this is aligned to the left. If you've removed other things frmo the the head it may make sense to break that up in submenus so those pieces of functionality is more discoverable.- Your commment functionality requires sign up to use, keeping it there may help lead to signs ups, but if you're designing this as an open source tool, maybe you're less interested in growth hacking, it might make sense to remove it from the header as well when the user isn't signed in (at the same time keeping it there signals to people weighing up your product that that feature exists.- you have 2 layers of headers, is it worth utilising horitonzal space for some of your buttons and put them in the right hand side?Hopefully you can feed the above back into your agent on a loop lol.reply

title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening (twitter.com/karpathy)
comments: https://xxcancel.com/karpathy/status/2109361546505966046
you are my hero

Don't think the 0.2% really are in agreement that "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt".The divide seems to be between people who think you may need to understand the codebase for maintenance, potential future token costs, optimisation, code erosion & being wary of the assumptions/mistakes that they have seen LLMs make, and people who don't review code and are confident that the AI has made no mistakes and will be available for next-to-nothing forever.It's certainly allowing the latter to move fast... but will their clients be happy if/when they break things.  We'll find out soon, I'm sure.reply

It's not that we're assuming the AI has made no mistakes. It's that we're confident in the general capability of the models such that we're willing to accept it'll make some mistakes, but working together with it, we'll still achieve our end goals.I presume you also know your own code has mistakes, too? You wouldn't refuse to even look at the code of a colleague who has ever made a coding mistake, would you?reply

My colleagues write 10x less code for the same tasks (when they don't (ab)use AI) and don't reach past abstraction boundaries so that it's possible to actually reason about and review their work. When the problems get hard, they apply more care and attention to detail. Even if LLMs had the same bug rate per SLOC (IME it's higher), and even if those bugs were the same severity (IME they're worse), you'd still expect 10x bugs just because they can't be arsed to write a reasonable amount of code.Almost all my code nowadays is AI-written, with me just contributing the concurrent data structures, a good spec, and some review and touch-up. I'm not _that_ much of a Luddite about this stuff. I'm not blind either though. Your "working together" comment does a lot of heavy lifting when arguing against a post saying that leaving the LLM to its own devices is a bad idea.reply

If you are reaching past abstraction boundaries and making spaghetti code you are holding it wrong.We create higher quality, more testable code, with less complexity and less LOC per functional unit than we ever did with humans.  By a long stretch.Documentation driven development with constant naive review, delta review, documentation/code coherence review agents, test coverage review agents, development standards and architecture review, etc. We write code once, then review and revise each module from a variety of different paradigms until every line, every construct, every function, every interface is optimally constructed and documented. Agents learn to write code that passes with less flags by having it pushed back to them until it passes, and revising their learnings files.By the time code makes it to a commit it’s been brought into compliance from a variety of perspectives and tested as completely as possible, along with mutants that test the tests. By the time it gets to a merge gate, most code has been through at least 50 reviews. Then we periodically sweep the entire codebase for cruft, vulnerabilities, corner cases, etc. If we find smells or clever sections, they are eradicated.In total, the hot paths and critical infrastructure sees hundreds of reviews against thousands of rules and best practices.Sure, it’s expensive, but still 1/4 the cost of regular development, and much, much fewer bugs.Unfortunately, most people are out there just vibin, even at the big corps, and it’s a dumpster fire.It’s easy to produce garbage software, but it’s not mandatory.reply

How is that 1/4th the cost of the regular development? Did your pre-AI code ever hit 50 reviews? If not, it’s impossible that it was slower. If you are talking about agent reviews, it’s not expensive.Which is it?reply

I'm not the guy you're responding to, but I have the same experience. If anything, 1/4 cost underestimates the savings.The analogy is like pointing out that you can have a robot vacuum clean your floors every day. Before the robot, you'd do it maybe once a week, just no time - "too expensive" to even think about doing it daily. The robot makes it happen all the time for a tiny, tiny fraction of the cost.reply

This is a different argument from Karpathy's prompt-and-forget one.I personally have had good success with using agents as virtual pair programmers following some simple rules for how to make that process productive, but that is a very, very different approach. One that recognizes that both humans and agents are prone to errors and attempts to mitigate the problem rather than expecting it will magically work out through the power of AI.reply

I think of it in generational terms. Opus 3 required me to prompt and edit, iterating over functions almost one at a time. Opus 4 started to show agentic capacity but it largely bloated code and still needed frequent course corrections. If it churned for more than 15-20 minutes you knew something was off.Opus 5 takes that and changes the game. A simple prompt goes through research, design, verification, review and self-corrects constantly. Agentic workflows can run for days without stopping, without losing the thread or devolving into slop.I can’t even imagine what Opus 6 is going to bring.The biggest thing holding AI back is people. People can only change so fast and yet AI doesn’t care. It just keeps accelerating.

title: Terence Tao: Math 2.0 [pdf] (teorth.github.io)
comments: I work in drug discovery and AI and his slide about cancer medicine isn't very well informed.  We have models and narratives about how drugs work, but they are woefully incomplete.I ask nearly every doctor/researched in the medical field: if you had a AI-created drug that tremendously improved cancer treatment outcomes for your patient, would you hesitate to prescribe it because nobody understood how it worked?   I have yet to hear "yes, I would hesitate", most people say "it would be cruel to deny a person a treatment that worked".I think Tao is focusing too much on second order effects of AI on math and other fields; humans are terrible at reasoning about second order effects, especially ones that are happening dynamically, in real time, using the most advanced mathematical models the world has yet created.reply

> [...] would you hesitate to prescribe it because nobody understood how it worked? I have yet to hear "yes, I would hesitate", most people say "it would be cruel to deny a person a treatment that worked".I feel like the way you frame the question makes answering it very easy but oversimplifies the reality.In a situation where an AI suggests a treatment to you without explanation and it appears to work, probably you can't even determine that the improved outcome is due to the drug or due to randomness (yes there are really rare cases where people recovered from stage 4 cancer). Especially if it's a personalized drug.If in this hypothetical world "it works on the patients I've tried it on" is good enough to try the drug, and you're willing to potentially cause harm if it doesn't work, then what's the line between science and pseudoscience/quack medicine? Every treatment surely "works" in at least some cases. So wouldn't it be cruel to deny the patient a try at every last treatment that has ever worked for someone in the past, including practices like bloodletting, acupuncture, etc? Would you give all of your patients this?I really would be curious why you would say no to some treatments and not others. Would it be because a study on the treatment shows it improves patient outcomes in some statistically significant way? But statistical significance isn't a guarantee that the effect is real. Not to mention there can't be a study like that if this is some personalized medicine that was just generated by the AI.Everyone wants the patient to survive but making correct decisions under uncertainty is not easy, I'm sure you know this.reply

I also work in drug discovery, and I completely agree; the extent to which the actual causal mechanisms of the efficacy of many drugs is woefully short of some human-appreciable first-principles based explanation. The point is especially undercut by hypothetically suggesting that this drug /does/ in fact pass stage 3 trials, at which point I can't fathom anyone would have a problem advancing it.Really wish he had chosen a different example; this particular bullet point has been making the rounds on X/twitter to paint Tao as an example of some sort of gatekeeping luddite who would deny the world a post-abundance future in order to maintain the prestige of his particular career path...which is tough because I cannot think of a more responsible steward of our inevitable AI future than Tao at the moment.reply

title: Passkeys are a trap (nonfunctional.substack.com)
comments: Note that attestation can only be required during credential registration; at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration. And browsers will throw up a permission prompt if a website requests attestation. Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt? I very much doubt it, since Apple's passkey implementation doesn't support attestation.Therefore, the author's scenario that sites will wait until most of their users are using attested passkeys and then "flip the switch and start rejecting non-attested passkeys" isn't very plausible.Attestation is certainly a stain on the WebAuthn spec, and it would have been better if Chrome and Firefox didn't support attestation (unless perhaps the browser is enrolled in enterprise management), but this blog post is presenting a hypothetical and unlikely scenario. That's not a good enough reason to recommend TOTP instead, given that TOTP is vulnerable to phishing and passkeys aren't.If consumer-facing sites start requesting attestation when registering passkeys, they deserve to be vigorously called out, and maybe then the recommendation to use passkeys should be revisited.  But until that happens, don't tell people not to use passkeys.reply

> at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration.Of course it is, the site will reject the passkey and require you to create one that is attested.>  Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt?They could start tomorrow.> a hypothetical and unlikely scenario.You have not been paying attention, that scenario is where this whole thing is building towards.> If consumer-facing sites start requesting attestation when registering passkeys, they deserve to be vigorously called outIt's going to be the banks first.Why called out, it's all for your safety, to make sure you are not using an insecure client that might leak your data.reply

I don't know if you've noticed, but when Claude Code, Codex, or any other agent needs to find code, it runs grep. It searches your files for an exact string, reads a few results, and greps again until it finds what it wants. You pay tokens and wait for every round.That worked fine when repos were small. But codebases are growing fast, partly because agents now write so much of the code. Every grep round costs more than it did last month, whether you notice it or not.There's a second problem: grep only finds what you already know how to name. Ask it for "where we handle rate limits from the billing provider" and it gets 0% right on the first try, because it needs the exact string.So I built Pensieve. It's a local index of your code, documents, and past agent sessions. Any agent can query it over MCP and get the few files that matter on the first try. A few cents saved per lookup doesn't sound like much. It adds up over hundreds of lookups a day.Check out Pensieve!reply

> So I built Pensieve. It's a local index of your code, documents, and past agent sessions. Any agent can query it over MCP and get the few files that matter on the first tryWhat are the various ways Pensieve is superior to iterative grep? Is it just better "semantic" search instead of literal "grep"?Cache invalidation is hard - how does Pensieve address it?Your site says "Pensieve watches your folders, repos and agent sessions and re-indexes what changed. Uncommitted edits count, and every worktree is tracked by branch, so your agents never work from stale context." but you don't define what "stale context" is - if I'm exploring 3 different implmentations of the same concept across 3 different branches, which one is the "stale context"?Could you take a few minutes to explain the what and the how? Links to writeup to blog posts or files in your repo would be very helpful.Finally, can I use Pensieve with Paseo? What if I wanted to expose Pensieve's capability to my Paseo setup?reply

I also built something similar to solve this, but more aimed at inspecting the impact of changes to a concept - think a vertical slice or domain, or even a feature. Often the same thing might be referred to by similar, but slightly different names, or separate pieces of the codebase might not immediately look related when they do share dependencies. So symbols, phrases, and words are attached to concepts for either LLM-based or user-based querying via MCP.An indexer crawls the codebase and maps slices of code to concepts, then groups related concepts. You can inspect a concept to see things related to it, or ask about the impact of a change and see second-order changes required - things not so easy to see that are related by basic symbol linking (although it does use symbol linking - it heavily relies on Roslyn, since it's all C# focused).It also returns confidence scores with everything, which adjust based on a dozen or so factors like whether the user defined the concept or the concept was auto-generated during the code crawl. Low confidence score === fall back to grep.It was a super fun project and ended up being very useful, as much for people as the LLM. But, I'm not convinced it is materially better than grep in some ways and just haven't had the time to really focus on improving it.reply
